course: Daily Broiler Sales: Batch Production System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: When you sell broilers daily from a batch, every stage of the bird's life costs money. If you don't track expenses, you might think you're making profit when you're actually losing. For example, a farmer in Ghana buys 100 day-old chicks at 5 cedis each = 500 cedis. Feed for 6 weeks costs about 1,200 cedis. Vaccines and medication: 150 cedis. Bedding and heating: 200 cedis. Total expenses before selling: 2,050 cedis. If you sell all birds at 30 cedis each, you get 3,000 cedis. Your profit is 950 cedis. But if you forgot to count the 200 cedis for electricity and water, your real profit is only 750 cedis. That's a 21% drop! So tracking expenses at every stage tells you the true cost per bird. It helps you set the right selling price. It shows where you can cut costs without harming the birds. For daily sales, you need to know your break-even point: how many birds you must sell each day to cover costs. Suppose fixed costs (rent, labour) are 300 cedis per week. Variable cost per bird is 20.5 cedis (2,050 total / 100 birds). If you sell a bird at 30 cedis, your contribution per bird is 9.5 cedis. To cover 300 cedis fixed, you need 300 / 9.5 = 32 birds per week, about 5 birds per day. Without this calculation, you might sell too few and lose money. In Africa, many small-scale broiler farmers fail because they mix personal money with business money. They spend sales money on transport or airtime and then can't buy feed. This module will teach you simple tools to record every expense, from chick purchase to the last day of sales. You will learn to use a notebook, a calculator, and a simple table. By the end, you will know exactly how much each bird costs you and how to price for profit. Remember: profit is not what you receive; it's what you keep after all expenses.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To track expenses at every stage, you don't need expensive software. A simple exercise book, a pen, and a basic calculator will do. But you must be disciplined. Here are the tools and materials you need: 1) A hardcover notebook (cost: 500 naira or 10 cedis) to record daily expenses. Divide each page into columns: Date, Item, Quantity, Unit Price, Total, Stage (e.g., brooding, growing, finishing). 2) A calculator (cost: 1,500 naira) for quick addition. 3) A folder or envelope to keep all receipts. Even if you buy from a local market without receipts, write a small note and keep it. 4) A marker to label feed bags and medication. 5) A scale (cost: 5,000 naira) to weigh feed and birds. You need to know how much feed you use per bird. 6) A record book for daily sales. This is separate from expenses. You must record how many birds sold, at what price, and to whom. 7) A simple phone with calculator and calendar. You can use it to set reminders for vaccination and feed purchase. 8) A chart on the wall showing the batch timeline: week 1-2 brooding, week 3-4 growing, week 5-6 finishing. This helps you allocate expenses correctly. For example, brooding stage uses more electricity for heat lamps. Growing stage uses more feed. Finishing stage uses more water and labour for cleaning. If you don't have a scale, you can use a known container. For instance, a 10-litre bucket holds about 8 kg of feed. But a scale is better. Also, keep a small cash box for daily sales money. Do not mix it with your personal money. At the end of each day, count the money and write it down. If you can afford it, buy a receipt book (cost: 1,000 naira) to give to customers. This builds trust and helps you track sales. Finally, a simple calculator app on your phone can work, but a physical calculator is faster and doesn't need data. Total cost of these tools: about 8,000 naira or 150 cedis. That is a small investment to protect your profit.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps to track expenses at every stage of your broiler batch. Step 1: Before you buy chicks, create a budget. Write down all expected expenses: chicks, feed, vaccines, bedding, heating, water, labour, rent, transport, and miscellaneous. For 100 chicks, a sample budget: chicks 500 cedis, feed 1,200 cedis, vaccines 150 cedis, bedding 100 cedis, heating 100 cedis, water 50 cedis, labour 200 cedis, rent 100 cedis, transport 50 cedis, misc 50 cedis. Total = 2,500 cedis. Step 2: As you spend, record every expense immediately. Use your notebook. Write date, item, quantity, unit price, total, and stage. For example, on Day 1: 100 chicks at 5 cedis = 500 cedis (brooding stage). On Day 3: 2 bags of broiler starter at 300 cedis = 600 cedis (brooding). Step 3: At the end of each week, total your expenses by stage. Use a calculator. Write the weekly total. Step 4: Calculate cost per bird so far. Divide total expenses by number of surviving birds. If you started with 100 and 5 died, you have 95 birds. If expenses are 1,000 cedis, cost per bird = 10.53 cedis. Step 5: Compare with your selling price. If you plan to sell at 30 cedis, your margin is 19.47 cedis per bird. But remember, you still have future expenses. Step 6: Adjust your spending. If feed is costing more than budgeted, find a cheaper supplier or reduce waste. If mortality is high, check your management. Step 7: At the end of the batch, calculate total expenses and total revenue. Profit = revenue - expenses. Also calculate profit per bird. Step 8: Use this data to plan your next batch. If you made 800 cedis profit on 100 birds, you know you can scale up to 200 birds and expect about 1,600 cedis profit, if costs remain the same. But watch for diseconomies of scale. For daily sales, you need to know your daily break-even. Suppose your total expenses for the batch are 2,500 cedis and you expect to sell 100 birds over 20 days. Your average cost per bird is 25 cedis. If you sell at 30 cedis, you make 5 cedis per bird. To cover daily fixed costs of 20 cedis, you need to sell 4 birds per day. Keep a daily sales record and compare with expenses. If you sell less than 4 birds, you are losing money that day. This step-by-step method works for any size farm.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Many broiler farmers make mistakes that hide their true expenses. Here are common ones and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Not recording small expenses. You buy a 50 naira sachet of water for the birds or pay 100 naira for transport. You forget to write it down. Over a month, these small amounts add up to 3,000 naira. Fix: Keep a small notebook in your pocket. Write every expense, no matter how small. Mistake 2: Mixing personal and business money. You take 500 naira from sales to buy airtime. You don't record it as an expense. At the end, your profit looks higher than it is. Fix: Keep separate boxes or envelopes. One for business, one for personal. Pay yourself a fixed salary from the business. Mistake 3: Forgetting depreciation. Your feeder, drinker, and heat lamp wear out. If you don't set aside money for replacement, you will have a big expense later. Fix: Estimate the life of each tool. If a feeder costs 1,000 naira and lasts 10 batches, charge 100 naira per batch as depreciation. Mistake 4: Not counting your own labour. You work 3 hours daily. If you paid someone, it would cost 200 naira per day. Fix: Include a fair wage for yourself in expenses. This shows the true cost. Mistake 5: Using average costs instead of actual. You assume feed costs 300 naira per bag, but prices change. Fix: Record actual price each time you buy. Mistake 6: Ignoring mortality. If 10 birds die, you still spent money on their feed and vaccines. That cost must be spread over the surviving birds. Fix: Calculate cost per surviving bird, not per chick bought. Mistake 7: Not tracking sales daily. You sell 10 birds on Monday and 5 on Tuesday, but you only record weekly. You can't see daily profit. Fix: Use a daily sales sheet. Write number sold, price, and total. Mistake 8: Forgetting overheads like rent, electricity, and water. Fix: Allocate a portion of these to each batch. If rent is 1,000 naira per month and your batch lasts 6 weeks, charge 1,500 naira to the batch. Mistake 9: Not reviewing expenses. You keep records but never look at them. Fix: At the end of each week, review your notebook. Identify the biggest expense. Can you reduce it? For example, buy feed in bulk to get a discount. Mistake 10: Using guesswork for pricing. You sell at 30 naira because your neighbour does. But your costs might be higher. Fix: Calculate your break-even price and add a profit margin. These fixes will make your expense tracking accurate and your business profitable.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Tracking expenses is not just about numbers; it's about safety and best practices that protect your health, your birds, and your money. First, safety when handling money and records. Keep your record book and cash in a safe place, away from dampness and pests. If you use a phone, back up your records weekly. Never leave cash lying around. Deposit sales money in a bank or mobile money account as soon as possible. This reduces theft risk. Second, safety when handling feed and chemicals. Wear gloves and a nose mask when mixing feed or administering vaccines. Store feed in a dry, raised place to prevent mold. Moldy feed can kill birds and waste money. Third, best practice: keep a separate record for each batch. Label it with the start date and number of chicks. This helps you compare batches. Fourth, use a simple accounting method called 'cash accounting'. Record money when it comes in and when it goes out. Don't count unpaid debts as income. Fifth, do a monthly reconciliation. Count your cash, add money in mobile money, and compare with your records. If there is a difference, find out why. Sixth, train your workers. If you have helpers, teach them to record expenses. Give them a small notebook. Seventh, use technology wisely. If you have a smartphone, use a free app like 'Poultry Manager' or 'Farm Records'. But don't rely on it alone; keep a paper backup. Eighth, maintain a healthy environment. Clean water and proper ventilation reduce disease, which reduces medication expenses. Ninth, plan for emergencies. Keep a small fund for unexpected costs like disease outbreak or price hike. Tenth, review your expenses with a mentor or fellow farmer. Join a local poultry association. Share your records and learn from others. Eleventh, always calculate your cost per bird before setting price. Don't sell below cost. Twelfth, pay yourself a salary. This prevents you from eating into business capital. Thirteenth, keep personal and business expenses separate. Use different wallets or bank accounts. Fourteenth, take a photo of receipts and store them in a folder on your phone. Fifteenth, at the end of the batch, write a one-page report: total expenses, total revenue, profit, and lessons learned. This becomes your guide for the next batch. Following these safety and best practices will make your broiler business sustainable and profitable.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to practice. This exercise will help you apply what you learned about tracking expenses at every stage. You will need a notebook, pen, calculator, and the prices from your local market. Follow these steps: 1) Imagine you are starting a batch of 50 broiler chicks. Write down all expected expenses for a 6-week cycle. Use real prices from your area. For example, in Nigeria: chicks 50 x 800 naira = 40,000 naira. Feed: 4 bags starter at 8,000 = 32,000; 6 bags finisher at 7,500 = 45,000. Vaccines: 2,000. Bedding: 1,500. Heating: 3,000. Water: 1,000. Labour: 5,000. Rent: 2,000. Transport: 1,500. Misc: 1,000. Total = 134,000 naira. 2) Create a table with columns: Date, Item, Quantity, Unit Price, Total, Stage. Fill in the first week's expenses as if you are buying and starting. 3) Calculate cost per chick at the end of week 1. Assume no mortality. Cost per chick = total week 1 expenses / 50. 4) Now imagine that in week 2, you spend 15,000 naira on feed and 500 naira on water. Two chicks die. Update your total expenses and calculate cost per surviving chick. 5) Continue for weeks 3 to 6. Make up realistic expenses. At the end of week 6, you have 48 birds. Total expenses = 134,000 naira (if no extra). Cost per bird = 134,000 / 48 = 2,791.67 naira. 6) You plan to sell at 3,500 naira per bird. Calculate total revenue if you sell all 48 birds: 48 x 3,500 = 168,000 naira. Profit = 168,000 - 134,000 = 34,000 naira. Profit per bird = 34,000 / 48 = 708.33 naira. 7) Now calculate break-even sales per day. Suppose you want to sell over 20 days. Fixed costs per day: rent and labour = (2,000 + 5,000) / 20 = 350 naira per day. Variable cost per bird = (134,000 - 7,000) / 48 = 2,645.83 naira. Contribution per bird = 3,500 - 2,645.83 = 854.17 naira. Break-even birds per day = 350 / 854.17 = 0.41, so you need to sell at least 1 bird per day to cover fixed costs. But to make profit, you need to sell more. 8) Write a short report: What was your biggest expense? How could you reduce it? For example, buy feed in bulk to save 5%. What was your profit margin? 9) Finally, set a target for your next batch. If you want to double profit, how many birds will you raise? What changes will you make? Do this exercise with real numbers from your area. It will teach you to think like a business person, not just a farmer.

quiz.q: Why is it important to track expenses at every stage of broiler production?
options: A) To know the true cost per bird and set the right selling price
C) To increase the number of birds you can raise
quiz.explanation: Tracking expenses reveals the actual cost per bird, helping you price for profit.

quiz.q: What is the break-even point in broiler sales?
options: A) The number of birds you must sell to cover all costs
B) The price at which you sell each bird
C) The total number of birds in a batch
D) The weight of the birds at market age
quiz.explanation: Break-even is the sales volume needed to cover fixed and variable costs.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fixed cost in broiler production?
options: C) Rent for the poultry house
quiz.explanation: Rent does not change with the number of birds raised, so it is a fixed cost.

quiz.q: If you buy 100 chicks at 5 cedis each, what is the total cost?
quiz.explanation: 100 multiplied by 5 cedis equals 500 cedis.

quiz.q: What is the first step in tracking expenses?
quiz.explanation: A budget lists all expected expenses before you start spending.

quiz.q: Which tool is most essential for recording daily expenses?
quiz.explanation: A notebook and pen are cheap, reliable, and do not need electricity or data.

quiz.q: Why should you keep personal and business money separate?
options: A) To avoid confusion and know true profit
B) To hide money from family
C) To qualify for a loan
quiz.explanation: Mixing money makes it impossible to calculate accurate profit.

quiz.q: What is depreciation in broiler production?
options: A) The loss of value of equipment over time
C) The decrease in feed quality
D) The drop in market price
quiz.explanation: Depreciation is the wear and tear of tools like feeders and drinkers.

quiz.q: If total expenses are 2,000 cedis and you have 80 surviving birds, what is the cost per bird?
quiz.explanation: 2000 divided by 80 equals 25 cedis per bird.

quiz.q: Which stage of broiler production uses the most feed?
quiz.explanation: Finishing stage birds eat more feed as they grow larger.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when tracking expenses?
options: B) Forgetting to record small expenses
quiz.explanation: Small expenses add up and can significantly affect profit if ignored.

quiz.q: How can you fix the mistake of not counting your own labour?
options: B) Include a fair wage for yourself in expenses
quiz.explanation: Your time has value; including it shows the true cost of production.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calculate cost per surviving bird?
options: A) Because dead birds still cost money
B) Because surviving birds are heavier
quiz.explanation: Expenses on dead birds must be covered by the surviving birds.

quiz.q: What is a best practice for storing feed?
options: B) In a dry, raised place
quiz.explanation: A dry, raised place prevents mold and pest damage.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a separate record for each batch?
options: A) To compare performance between batches
quiz.explanation: Comparing batches helps you identify what works and what doesn't.

quiz.q: What is cash accounting?
options: A) Recording money when it is received or paid
B) Recording money only when you have cash
C) Counting cash at the end of the day
quiz.explanation: Cash accounting records transactions when cash changes hands.

quiz.q: How often should you reconcile your cash records?
quiz.explanation: Monthly reconciliation helps catch errors and theft.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of joining a poultry association?
options: A) You can share records and learn from others
C) You don't need to track expenses
D) You can sell at higher prices
quiz.explanation: Associations provide mentorship and collective bargaining power.

quiz.q: In the practical exercise, if total expenses are 134,000 naira and you have 48 birds, what is the cost per bird?
quiz.explanation: 134,000 divided by 48 equals approximately 2,791.67 naira.

quiz.q: If you sell 48 birds at 3,500 naira each, what is total revenue?
quiz.explanation: 48 multiplied by 3,500 equals 168,000 naira.

quiz.q: What is profit if revenue is 168,000 naira and expenses are 134,000 naira?
quiz.explanation: 168,000 minus 134,000 equals 34,000 naira.

quiz.q: How do you calculate break-even birds per day?
options: A) Fixed costs per day divided by contribution per bird
B) Total expenses divided by number of birds
C) Selling price minus cost price
D) Total revenue divided by days
quiz.explanation: Break-even = fixed costs per day / (selling price - variable cost per bird).

quiz.q: Why should you set aside a fund for emergencies?
options: A) To cover unexpected costs like disease outbreak
quiz.explanation: Emergencies can disrupt production if you have no reserve.

quiz.q: What is a good way to reduce feed expenses?
options: A) Buy in bulk to get discounts
B) Feed less to the birds
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying reduces unit cost without harming bird health.

quiz.q: What should you do with receipts?
options: A) Keep them in a folder or take photos
quiz.explanation: Receipts provide proof of expenses for record-keeping.

quiz.q: Why is it important to review expenses weekly?
options: A) To identify overspending and adjust
quiz.explanation: Weekly review allows timely corrective action.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in pricing?
options: A) Using guesswork based on neighbours' prices
quiz.explanation: Your costs may differ, so base price on your own calculations.

quiz.q: What does a one-page batch report include?
options: A) Total expenses, revenue, profit, and lessons learned
C) Only the number of birds
quiz.explanation: A complete report summarises all key financial and operational data.

quiz.q: Why is it important to pay yourself a salary?
options: A) To prevent eating into business capital
quiz.explanation: A salary separates personal income from business capital.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of Module 11?
options: A) To teach you to track expenses at every stage for profit
B) To teach you to raise broilers without feeding them
C) To teach you to sell at any price
D) To teach you to ignore costs
quiz.explanation: The module focuses on expense tracking to ensure profitability.
